correctness.rationale: The eight-state transition matrix is derived from unimodular Stern updates. Its exact characteristic polynomial and squarefree annihilator give a simple uniform eigenvalue 2 and second spectral modulus sqrt(2); aligned-block decomposition proves the global O(sqrt(N)) estimate. Three symmetric state classes give the exact order-two level recurrence; nonzero complex eigenmodes and a dyadic endpoint difference prove positive normalized limsup. A from-scratch exact integer verifier reconstructed the matrix and checked the polynomial identities, 17 dyadic levels and 131,072 prefixes.

originality.rationale: Deshouillers--Schinzel (2019), full eight-page primary paper, already implies density 1/4; that part is explicitly not claimed new. Its general Perron--Frobenius automaton theorem is qualitative: no sharp error, explicit three-term fluctuation recurrence, or nonzero sharp limsup is stated in its theorems or proof. The 2017 logarithmic-statistics paper treats a different observable. OEIS A002487 records basic sequence values, not these analytic bounds. Searches of published mathematical records and published-finding corpus returned no equivalent same-statement result; see structured comparisons and residual risks.
residual_risks: Unindexed older work or OEIS-linked literature may explicitly compute the same modulus-three recurrence.
Because the result follows by a small exact spectral calculation from the published automaton, another source may present the sharp bound as an unstated but readily derivable corollary.
The 2017 statistical-distribution preprint was read selectively, not exhaustively over all pages; its principal stated scope is different.

value.rationale: The previously established modular density has no quantitative convergence rate in the motivating primary paper. The first nontrivial odd modulus exhibits an exact oscillatory spectrum, and the proof determines the optimal power of N uniformly over all cutoffs, with a matching lower limsup. This is a natural quantitative strengthening of a published distribution theorem, rather than a repetition of its already-known density.
